<reason>A ran a disciplined, sharp case built on one fork: either youth limits require ID for every adult, or they collapse into the opt-in platform controls that already exist. A turned B's toll-collector line and used B's own "500 purchases" example well. But B dissolved the fork under direct pressure: when A asked whether a 13-year-old who typed "18" could beat the limit, B answered honestly (yes) and showed its case never relied on an age flag—defaults bind everyone, and only adults seeking to remove friction verify. A's later claim that this means "every adult who wants to buy a skin proves their age" overstates B's model, since purchasing under defaults needs no ID. B also kept the "child nobody catches" pressure live across every round; A's answer that both models fail the account-sharing child only holds if the parent has actively verified to unlock, whereas A's platform lock is off by default on adult accounts. That asymmetry—default-on versus opt-in—was B's cleanest route to victory and A never fully neutralized it. A won the geo-blocking exchange and had the more memorable phrasing, but B made the decisive comparison easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's A2 in Turn 7: conceding the age flag is defeatable and reframing defaults as protections that don't need to identify the child first, which converted A's strongest pressure question into a demonstration of why game-level defaults differ from platform gates.</best_rebuttal>
